messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Since the chemical exposure two years ago, Hans Weber, a 76-year-old divorced hotel manager, has lived as if danger could leak back into the air at any moment. The incident happened in the hotel basement during a maintenance problem with industrial cleaning agents. He had gone down himself when staff reported a sharp odor spreading near the laundry and supply area. What he remembers comes in jagged sections rather than a single narrative: the sting in his nose and throat, the sudden confusion among the staff, someone shouting to get out, the burning chemical smell seeming to coat the inside of his mouth. At times there is no picture at all, only a wave of terror that arrives in full force, as if his body has been dropped back into that basement without warning. When he tries to think about what happened, he can still smell it. Those disconnected, sensory fragments have come to feel more convincing to him than any reassurance afterward, and he has come to believe that his body cannot be trusted, that it reacts before he can understand anything, and that bad things can happen to him without any way to stop them.

That sense of bodily betrayal now shapes how he moves through each day. Hans says his body has become an enemy of sorts, launching into alarm even when he knows, intellectually, that he is safe. Because he no longer trusts his own internal signals, he is on guard even at home, listening for changes in the hum of appliances, a bang from a neighbor’s apartment, or any unexpected sound that might mean some new hazard has begun. Loud or sudden noises make him immediately tense and watchful. He has narrowed the world to a few places that feel tolerable, mostly a chair in his living room and a small office space at the hotel away from the lower floors, and even there he does not fully relax. The more on edge he feels, the more the event seems to return in fragments: not a clear memory, but a bodily surge, the chemical odor, flashes of the basement, enough to make the threat feel current rather than past.

In the months after the exposure, he began trying to manage these episodes in practical ways that made sense to him at the time. When the emotional force of the event came over him without warning, he would turn on the television at high volume or play loud music to drown out both the silence and his own mind. If he noticed himself beginning to think about the basement or the smell, he would monitor his thoughts closely, checking whether he was “losing it,” scanning for any sign that he was going crazy. He also stopped going near the site of the exposure. As hotel manager, he still oversees operations, but he now arranges for others to handle anything involving the basement, laundry, or chemical storage rooms. Staff have noticed that he reroutes his path through the building and becomes visibly tense if a maintenance issue is mentioned near that area. His efforts to avoid and override the experience have not settled it; if anything, the need to keep watch over his mind and steer clear of the site has deepened his conviction that he is fragile, that his body will react uncontrollably if he lets down his guard.

At home the same pattern has tightened. A sudden clatter in the kitchen or an unexpected sound from outside can leave him acutely alert, and in that state the sensory traces of the exposure return more easily—the smell, the fear, the sense of being overcome before he can act. Each recurrence seems to confirm what he has come to believe: that his body will keep reacting as though the danger is present, and that he is fundamentally helpless to prevent this. Once he starts checking his own mind for signs of breakdown, he feels less in command, not more. He turns the volume up higher, keeps himself busy with noise, and avoids anything that might remind him of the basement, but these habits have made his world smaller. He spends less time circulating through the hotel he once ran with confidence, and at home he lives inside a narrow perimeter of places he judges safe.

Hans finally agreed to seek help after a recent incident at work, when a sharp cleaning smell from a cart in the hallway stopped him in place and left him shaken for the rest of the day, unable to trust what his body was doing. What frightens him most is not only the memory of the exposure itself, but the belief that he could be overtaken again from the inside, by a body and mind he no longer feels he can rely on. What he wants, cautiously but clearly, is to be able to move through his hotel and his home without treating every sound, sensation, or passing smell as the beginning of another disaster.
